themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

lesson.title: Effects of Migration
lesson.summary: How migrants formed ethnic enclaves, how migration changed home societies, and how some receiving societies responded with exclusion.
learningGoals: Explain how and why new patterns of migration affected society from 1750 to 1900.
Explain why some receiving societies passed laws restricting immigration.
lesson.bigIdea: Migration created diverse communities around the world, changed gender roles at home, and provoked nativist laws in some receiving societies.
lesson.context: Migrants carried languages, religions, and foods with them. Their arrival changed both the places they went and the places they left.

sections.title: Ethnic enclaves and home societies

blocks.text: Migrants often formed ethnic enclaves, such as Chinese communities in Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and San Francisco, and Indian communities in East Africa and the Caribbean.
Most migrants were young men. Women in home societies, such as southern Italy and southern China, often took on more responsibility for farms and businesses.

sections.takeaway: Migration built diverse communities and changed family roles at home.

sections.title: Nativism and exclusion

blocks.text: Some receiving societies reacted with nativism, hostility toward immigrants. The United States passed the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882, and Australia adopted the White Australia Policy in 1901.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Economic competition and racial ideas led some workers and politicians to blame immigrants, which produced laws excluding them.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Exclusion laws targeted particular groups. The same countries welcomed many European immigrants.

sections.takeaway: Racial ideas shaped who receiving societies welcomed and excluded.

connections.title: Migration in the 1900s
connections.body: Unit 9 traces migration after 1900, including movement from former colonies to Europe.
connections.transferQuestion: How might patterns of migration change after empires end?
connections.feedback: Suggest a connection between former colonies and former imperial powers.
